title: Why Breakfast Matters
summary: Why the body and brain need breakfast after the long overnight fast, and which foods make a healthy breakfast that gives lasting energy.
poll: Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

versions.title: Eat in the Morning
versions.text:
You wake up. You are hungry. Why? You did not eat all night!

You slept for a long time. But your body did not stop. Your heart beat. You took breaths. Your body grew. All of that takes energy. Food gives you energy.

The first meal of the day is breakfast. The word means to break the fast. A fast is a long time with no food.

Breakfast helps your brain. It helps you focus in class. It helps you think. Kids who skip it can feel tired. They may get grumpy, too.

Some foods are best. Eggs and beans have protein. Protein helps you stay full. Bread made from whole wheat gives you fuel that lasts. Fruit is good, too. A few dates can help.

Some foods are not so good. Sweet cakes give a quick boost. But then you feel tired fast.

So eat a healthy breakfast. Then you will be set for the day!

versions.title: Eat in the Morning
versions.text:
You wake up. Your tummy rumbles. Why are you so hungry? You did not eat all night!

You slept for many hours. But your body kept working. Your heart kept beating. You kept breathing. Your body kept growing. All of this takes energy. Your body gets energy from food.

The first meal of the day is called breakfast. The word means to break the fast. A fast is a long time with no food.

Breakfast helps your brain work well. It helps you focus in class. It helps you think. It helps you remember. Some kids skip it. They may feel tired and grumpy.

Some foods are best for breakfast. Eggs, beans, milk, and labneh have protein. Protein helps you feel full. Whole wheat bread gives you energy. It lasts a long time. Fruit and a few dates are good, too.

Some foods are not as good. Sweet cakes and sugary cereal give a quick boost. But soon you feel tired again.

So eat a healthy breakfast each day. Then you will be ready to learn and play!

versions.title: Why Breakfast Matters
versions.text:
When you wake up in the morning, your stomach may rumble loudly. You might wonder why you are so hungry. The reason is simple: you have probably not eaten for ten hours or more!

Even while you sleep, your body keeps working. Your heart pumps blood, your lungs breathe, and your body repairs itself and grows. All of these jobs use energy, and the energy comes from the food you eat.

The first meal of the day is called breakfast. The word joins two smaller words, break and fast. A fast is a long period without food, so a morning meal breaks the fast of the night.

Your brain needs energy to concentrate. Many studies have found that children who eat breakfast find it easier to pay attention in class and remember what they learn. Children who skip breakfast may feel tired or grumpy, and they often feel very hungry long before lunch.

The best breakfasts combine different kinds of food. Eggs, beans, milk, and labneh contain protein, which helps you feel full longer. Whole wheat bread contains fiber, so its energy is released slowly and lasts through the morning. Fruit and dates add vitamins and other nutrients.

Some breakfast foods are less helpful. Sweet pastries and sugary cereals give a quick burst of energy, but that energy drops quickly, and you soon feel tired and hungry again.

A healthy breakfast does not have to be fancy. A boiled egg, a piece of whole wheat bread, and a glass of milk can help you start the day strong.

versions.title: Why Breakfast Matters
versions.text:
When you wake up in the morning, your stomach may rumble loudly, and you might wonder why you feel so ravenous. The explanation is straightforward: by the time you get out of bed, you have probably not eaten anything for ten hours or more.

Even while you are asleep, your body continues functioning without a pause. Your heart pumps blood, your lungs breathe, and your body repairs damaged tissue and grows, and all of these activities require energy. Much of that energy comes from glucose, a simple sugar that your body obtains by digesting the carbohydrates in the food you eat.

The first meal of the day is called breakfast, a word that combines two smaller words, break and fast. A fast is an extended period without food, so a morning meal literally breaks the overnight fast and refills the body's supply of fuel.

Your brain depends especially heavily on glucose, and it needs a steady supply in order to maintain concentration. Numerous studies have found that children who eat breakfast find it easier to pay attention in class and to remember new information. By contrast, children who skip breakfast may feel exhausted or irritable, and they frequently become extremely hungry long before lunch.

The most beneficial breakfasts combine several different categories of food. Eggs, beans, milk, and labneh contain protein, which helps you feel satisfied for longer. Whole wheat bread contains fiber, which slows digestion so that glucose enters the blood gradually and its energy lasts throughout the morning. Fruit and dates provide vitamins and other essential nutrients that help your body remain healthy.

Some popular breakfast foods are considerably less helpful. Sweet pastries and sugary cereals are usually made from refined flour and sugar, which the body digests very rapidly. They provide a quick burst of energy, but because that energy declines just as quickly, you soon feel tired and hungry again.

A nutritious breakfast does not need to be complicated or expensive. A boiled egg, a slice of whole wheat bread, a few dates, and a glass of milk can help you begin the day energetically, and preparing something simple the previous evening can make hectic mornings considerably easier.

versions.title: Why Breakfast Matters
versions.text:
Upon waking each morning, it is scarcely surprising that your stomach announces itself audibly, since by the time you climb out of bed you have typically gone without any food for ten hours or longer, the most extended interval of deprivation you experience throughout an ordinary day.

Even during sleep, the body never ceases its essential functions: the heart continues circulating blood, the lungs continue drawing breath, and damaged tissues undergo continuous repair and growth, and every one of these physiological processes demands energy, a substantial proportion of which derives from glucose, a simple sugar that the body obtains by digesting the carbohydrates present in previously consumed food.

The first meal of the day derives its name, breakfast, from the fusion of two smaller words, break and fast, since a fast denotes an extended period of abstention from food; a morning meal therefore literally breaks the overnight fast and replenishes the body's substantially diminished reserves of fuel.

The brain depends upon glucose with particular intensity and requires an essentially continuous supply in order to sustain concentration across the demands of a school day. Numerous peer-reviewed studies have established that children who consume breakfast find it considerably easier to maintain attention during lessons and to retain unfamiliar information presented to them. By contrast, children who forgo breakfast frequently report exhaustion or irritability and typically experience intense hunger long before the arrival of lunch, circumstances that often lead them toward less nutritious snacking later in the morning.

The most beneficial breakfasts characteristically combine several distinct categories of food. Eggs, legumes, milk, and labneh supply protein, which promotes a prolonged sensation of satiety, whereas whole wheat bread supplies fiber, which decelerates digestion so that glucose enters the bloodstream gradually and its associated energy persists throughout the morning rather than dissipating rapidly. Fruit and dates, meanwhile, contribute vitamins, minerals, and other essential nutrients that the body requires to maintain optimal health.

Certain popular breakfast foods, however, prove considerably less beneficial, since sweet pastries and sugary cereals are typically manufactured from refined flour and sugar, ingredients from which the coarser, slower-digesting components have been deliberately removed. The body digests such refined foods with remarkable rapidity, generating an immediate surge of energy that, precisely because it arrives so quickly, also dissipates with comparable speed, leaving the consumer sluggish and hungry again well before the next meal.

A genuinely nutritious breakfast, fortunately, need be neither elaborate nor expensive to prepare. A boiled egg, a slice of whole wheat bread, a handful of dates, and a glass of milk together provide sufficient fuel to begin the day with energy and focus, and preparing such modest provisions the previous evening can render even the most hectic mornings considerably more manageable. Cultivating this habit early in life represents a remarkably straightforward investment in both lifelong physical health and sustained academic achievement.

versions.title: Why Breakfast Matters
versions.text:
Upon waking each morning, it is scarcely surprising that your stomach announces itself audibly and insistently, since by the time you climb out of bed you have typically gone without any food for ten hours or longer, the most extended interval of nutritional deprivation you experience throughout an ordinary day.

Even during sleep, the body never ceases its essential physiological functions: the heart continues circulating blood tirelessly, the lungs continue drawing breath, and damaged tissues undergo continuous, incremental repair and growth, and every one of these processes demands a steady expenditure of energy, a substantial proportion of which derives from glucose, a simple sugar that the body obtains by digesting the carbohydrates present in previously consumed food.

The first meal of the day derives its designation, breakfast, from the fusion of two smaller words, break and fast, since a fast denotes an extended period of deliberate abstention from food; a morning meal therefore literally breaks the overnight fast and replenishes the body's substantially diminished reserves of readily available fuel.

The brain depends upon glucose with particular physiological intensity and requires an essentially uninterrupted supply in order to sustain the sharp concentration demanded by a typical school day. Numerous peer-reviewed studies have established, with considerable consistency, that children who consume breakfast find it markedly easier to maintain sustained attention during lessons and to retain unfamiliar information presented to them. By contrast, children who habitually forgo breakfast frequently report exhaustion or irritability and typically experience intense, distracting hunger long before the arrival of lunch, circumstances that often lead them toward less nutritious snacking choices later in the morning.

The most beneficial breakfasts characteristically combine several distinct categories of food in deliberate proportion. Eggs, legumes, milk, and labneh supply protein, which promotes a prolonged sensation of satiety and reduces the temptation to snack, whereas whole wheat bread supplies fiber, which decelerates digestion so that glucose enters the bloodstream gradually and incrementally, allowing its associated energy to persist throughout the entire morning rather than dissipating abruptly. Fruit and dates, meanwhile, contribute vitamins, minerals, and other essential nutrients that the body requires to sustain optimal physiological functioning.

Certain popular breakfast foods, however, prove considerably less beneficial nutritionally, since sweet pastries and sugary cereals are typically manufactured from refined flour and sugar, ingredients from which the coarser, slower-digesting components have been deliberately and industrially removed during processing. The body digests such refined foods with remarkable rapidity, generating an immediate surge of energy that, precisely because it arrives so abruptly, also dissipates with comparable speed, leaving the consumer sluggish, unfocused, and hungry again well before the arrival of the next scheduled meal.

A genuinely nutritious breakfast, fortunately, need be neither elaborate nor expensive to prepare on even the busiest morning. A boiled egg, a slice of whole wheat bread, a handful of dates, and a glass of milk together provide sufficient and well-balanced fuel to begin the day with sustained energy and mental focus, and preparing such modest provisions the previous evening can render even the most hectic mornings considerably more manageable for an entire household. Cultivating this habit early in life represents a remarkably straightforward and low-cost investment in both lifelong physical health and sustained academic achievement throughout one's school years.

questions.why: The last paragraph says a healthy breakfast does not need to be complicated, and gives a simple example.

wrong.A: The article shows simple, ordinary foods.
wrong.B: Milk is part of the example breakfast.
wrong.C: A boiled egg and bread are quick to prepare.

MID.prompt: Explain why a breakfast of eggs and whole wheat bread is better than a sugary pastry. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained the difference between the two breakfasts.
I used at least two details from the article.
I wrote in complete sentences and checked my spelling.
MID.modelAnswer: A breakfast of eggs and whole wheat bread is better than a sugary pastry because it gives your body steady, lasting energy instead of a quick burst that fades fast. The article explains that eggs contain protein, which helps you feel satisfied for longer, while whole wheat bread contains fiber, so its energy releases gradually through the whole morning. This steady supply of nutrients also helps your brain concentrate in class, but a sugary pastry gives a fast rise in energy that quickly falls, leaving you tired and hungry again before lunch.

keyWords.definition: a simple sugar that the body uses as its main fuel
keyWords.example: During the race, her muscles burned glucose for energy.

keyWords.definition: substances in food that the body needs to grow, repair itself, and stay healthy
keyWords.example: Spinach provides several important nutrients, including iron.

keyWords.definition: the part of plant foods that the body digests slowly, which helps digestion
keyWords.example: Lentil soup is rich in fiber and keeps you full.

keyWords.definition: the ability to keep your attention on one task
keyWords.example: The chess player's concentration did not break for an hour.

keyWords.definition: processed so that rough or natural parts are removed
keyWords.example: White flour is refined, so it has less fiber than whole wheat flour.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: A balanced breakfast refuels the body after the overnight fast and supports concentration and learning.
Glucose is harmful to the brain and should be avoided by children at breakfast.
Only children need to eat breakfast.
Refined foods are the healthiest choice in the morning.
questions.why: The article explains how breakfast restores fuel, especially glucose for the brain, and which foods give lasting energy.

wrong.B: Glucose is the body's main fuel; the article does not call it harmful.
wrong.C: The article focuses on children but does not say adults never need breakfast.
wrong.D: The article says refined foods are less beneficial.

questions.stem: According to the article, how does the body get glucose?
options: By breathing deeply while asleep
By digesting the carbohydrates in food
By sleeping a few hours longer
By drinking water
questions.why: The article says the body obtains glucose by digesting the carbohydrates in food.

wrong.A: Breathing is not how glucose is obtained.
wrong.C: Sleep uses energy; it does not supply glucose.
wrong.D: Water does not contain glucose.

questions.stem: What is the effect of fiber in whole wheat bread?
options: It makes glucose enter the blood quickly.
It removes all the protein from the bread.
It slows digestion so energy lasts longer.
It turns bread into sugar.
questions.why: The article says fiber slows digestion so glucose enters the bloodstream gradually and energy lasts.

wrong.A: Fiber slows, not speeds, the process.
wrong.D: The article does not say this.

questions.stem: In the article, the word refined describes flour that
options: has extra fiber added
is digested very slowly
comes straight from the field without any changes
has been processed so it is digested quickly
questions.why: The article links refined flour with foods the body digests very rapidly.

wrong.A: Refined flour has had parts removed, not added.
wrong.B: The article says refined foods are digested rapidly.

questions.stem: Why does the author explain what happens to the body during sleep before discussing food choices?
options: To show why the body needs to be refueled in the morning
To prove that sleep is unhealthy
To argue that children sleep too much and should wake earlier
To describe a dream
questions.why: Explaining that the body uses energy overnight sets up why breakfast is needed before the article discusses which foods are best.

wrong.B: The article does not call sleep unhealthy.
wrong.C: The article does not say children sleep too much.
wrong.D: No dream is described.

questions.stem: Which detail supports the claim that breakfast helps learning?
options: Dates are popular in Saudi Arabia.
Studies found children who eat breakfast pay attention and remember more easily.
Pastries are made from refined flour and sugar.
The word breakfast joins two words.
questions.why: The studies about attention and memory directly connect breakfast to learning.

wrong.A: Dates are a food example, not evidence about learning.
wrong.C: This is about pastries, not learning.
wrong.D: This explains the word, not learning.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about a breakfast of only sugary cereal?
options: It would keep a student alert until lunch.
It contains more protein than eggs.
It might leave a student sluggish by mid-morning.
It is the best choice before a test.
questions.why: Refined, sugary foods give a burst of energy that declines quickly, leaving you sluggish and hungry.

wrong.A: The article says the energy declines quickly.
wrong.B: Eggs are named as the protein source.
wrong.D: A food that leaves you sluggish would not be best before a test.

questions.stem: Why might the brain be especially affected by skipping breakfast?
options: The brain does not use energy.
The brain depends heavily on a steady supply of glucose.
The brain only works at night.
The brain stores large amounts of protein for the morning.
questions.why: The article states that the brain depends especially heavily on glucose and needs a continuous supply to concentrate.

wrong.A: The article says the brain needs energy.
wrong.D: The article does not say this.

HIGH.prompt: Some students say they are too busy to eat breakfast. Write a response that persuades them to eat it, using evidence from the article.
checklist: I used at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I answered the concern about being busy and used correct grammar and punctuation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Even if you feel too busy to eat breakfast, skipping it is likely costing you more time and energy than it saves. After ten or more hours without food, your brain is running low on the glucose it needs, and studies described in the article show that students who skip breakfast often feel tired, irritable, and far hungrier before lunch, which makes it harder to maintain concentration in class. A refined, sugary snack is not much better, since it causes your energy to spike and then crash quickly, but a simple combination of protein and fiber-rich nutrients, like a boiled egg, whole wheat bread, and a few dates, can be prepared the night before in only a few minutes. A few minutes spent eating breakfast is a small price for the steady energy and focus it gives you the rest of the morning.
